claimBoundary: Candidate explanations only. None is a PAL invariant, Core law, architecture requirement, owner obligation or promotion authority.

families.claim: Persistence and future availability are the dominant causes of later adaptive value.
predictions: implemented or durably retained changes should usually outperform absent changes in later work
change type and owner placement should add relatively little once the change remains available
falsifiers: many persistent changes have no independent consumer or outcome gain
fresh reconstruction or deletion performs as well or better than retained state/capability

families.claim: Recursive depth is the dominant cause of compounding: method and meta-selection changes should transfer more reliably than state, capability or policy changes.
predictions: method/meta-selection changes show more independent downstream consumers than shallower change classes
change-depth rank predicts transfer even after domain and mechanism differences
falsifiers: deep changes fail while shallow procedural/knowledge changes transfer
mechanism/observability explains outcomes better than depth

families.claim: Durable adaptive value comes primarily from placing future-model-robust responsibilities into the substrate with structural advantage while preserving owner-native truth and Agent semantic choice.
predictions: candidates with repeated burden, clear owner, strong simpler-baseline failure and future-model-robust invariant survive contraction
model-contingent convenience layers and duplicate authorities are localized/deleted even when large or useful
successful cross-owner transfer often externalizes deterministic/mechanical burden rather than semantic judgment
falsifiers: large durable successes depend mainly on current-model convenience with no stable responsibility
responsibility-placement features fail to predict historical dispositions better than implementation/persistence baselines
families.promotionCeiling: candidate PAL mechanism; already supported as Agent-first law but PAL generalization unproven

families.claim: Transfer succeeds mainly when the effect of a retained prior is locally observable, evaluator-aligned and causally close enough for reliable credit assignment.
predictions: procedural priors with immediate exact evidence transfer more reliably than long-horizon strategic directives
partial failures concentrate at the boundary where exact substrate output becomes model interpretation or delayed outcome
abstraction alone is insufficient without observable discriminating feedback
falsifiers: long-horizon weakly observable priors transfer as reliably as local verifiable procedures
transfer is explained better by domain similarity or abstraction level across held-out cases

families.claim: The main current bottleneck in recursive improvement is generating sufficiently diverse causal hypotheses/interventions; selection quality is secondary once a rich candidate set exists.
predictions: multiple independently generated variants under matched budget increase oracle-scored solution quality or falsifier discovery
historical failures frequently reflect missing alternatives rather than bad selection among available alternatives
falsifiers: matched-budget variant generation adds redundancy but not held-out value
selection/credit failures dominate even with diverse candidate sets

families.claim: Beneficial compounding requires explicit negative-feedback mechanisms such as falsification, rollback, deletion, strong baselines and authority separation; positive feedback alone is not evidence of adaptation quality.
predictions: successful reform lineages contain repeated contraction/null/deletion events before stable promotion
removing independent oracle or rollback pressure increases false retention or self-confirming success
systems that only retain positive changes accumulate dead complexity or Goodhart behavior
falsifiers: successful long-horizon reforms compound without meaningful negative selection
regulation adds cost but does not change false-retention/transfer outcomes under matched experiments
